The book lists low PaO2 and high PaCO2 on ABG.
The book lists a low FEV1/FVC ratio and high lung volumes from air trapping.
Small lung volumes are the opposite of the hyperinflation seen in emphysema.
Emphysema causes low oxygen and retained CO2, not the reverse.
questions.clue: Air trapping and impaired gas exchange.
questions.priority: Interpret diagnostic results in emphysema.

questions.stem: A client with emphysema has trouble clearing secretions. Which nursing actions help maintain airway clearance? Select all that apply.
options: Use a humidifier
Teach the client to suppress coughing
Teach controlled coughing
Keep the client flat after meals
Coach pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing
rationales: Correct. A humidifier is listed under maintaining airway clearance.
Incorrect. The book teaches controlled coughing, not cough suppression.
Correct. Controlled coughing is listed under maintaining airway clearance.
Incorrect. The book recommends high Fowler's or orthopneic positioning.
Correct. Pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing are listed under maintaining airway clearance.
questions.clue: Independent nursing actions: maintain airway clearance.
questions.priority: Support airway clearance with humidity, controlled coughing and breathing techniques.

questions.stem: A client with severe emphysema is being discharged. Which actions should the nurse include to prevent infection? Select all that apply.
options: Screen visitors for illness
Invite a grandchild who has a cold to visit
Avoid crowds
Wait until sputum turns green before calling about an infection
Get infections treated promptly
rationales: Correct. Screening visitors is listed under infection prevention.
Incorrect. Exposure to a person with a respiratory infection increases risk.
Correct. Avoiding crowds is listed under infection prevention.
Incorrect. The book calls for prompt treatment of infections to reduce bronchospasm and secretions.
Correct. Treating infections promptly is a listed collaborative intervention.
questions.clue: Infection prevention in emphysema.
questions.priority: Protect the client with emphysema from respiratory infection.

questions.stem: A client with severe emphysema asks the provider about surgery. Which surgical options does the book list for select clients? Select all that apply.
options: Bullectomy
Thoracentesis
Lung volume reduction surgery
IVC filter placement
Lung transplant
rationales: Correct. Bullectomy is listed.
Incorrect. Thoracentesis removes pleural fluid; it is not an emphysema surgery.
Correct. Lung volume reduction surgery is listed.
Incorrect. An IVC filter is used for PE, not emphysema.
Correct. Lung transplant is listed and improves quality of life.
questions.clue: Surgical options for select clients.
questions.priority: Coordinate referrals for surgical options in advanced disease.

questions.stem: A client with emphysema becomes restless and anxious and has new trouble following directions. What should the nurse consider first?
options: Situational anxiety only, so offer a relaxation recording
Low oxygen, since confusion and restlessness can be signs of oxygen deficiency
Depression related to role loss
A reaction to having too many visitors
rationales: Incorrect. Assuming anxiety alone could miss hypoxemia.
Correct. The book lists confusion, restlessness and mental status changes as oxygen deficiency signs; a physical cause must be ruled out before treating this as anxiety.
Incorrect. Depression is a concern in emphysema, but new confusion needs an oxygen check first.
Incorrect. Visitors do not explain new confusion.
questions.clue: New restlessness and confusion.
questions.priority: Rule out hypoxia before attributing cognitive change to anxiety.

questions.stem: A client with severe emphysema who had to retire early says, "I used to support my family. Now I can't do anything." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "At least you have more free time now."
"Everyone with emphysema has to stop working eventually."
"Let's focus on your breathing exercises instead."
"Losing your role at work is a big change. Tell me more about how it has affected you."
rationales: Incorrect. This minimizes the client's loss.
Incorrect. This generalizes and dismisses the client's feelings.
Incorrect. This changes the subject and blocks communication.
Correct. The book lists occupational and role loss as a psychosocial concern; an open response lets the client express feelings and lets the nurse assess for depression.
questions.clue: Expressed loss of role and purpose.
questions.priority: Use therapeutic communication to address role loss.

questions.stem: Which change best explains the increased work of breathing in pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Loss of elastic recoil traps air in the alveoli
IgE-driven bronchospasm narrows the airways
Fluid collects between the visceral and parietal pleura
Scarred alveoli lower lung compliance and increase elastic recoil
rationales: Incorrect. Air trapping from lost elasticity describes emphysema.
Incorrect. IgE-driven bronchospasm describes allergic asthma.
Incorrect. Fluid between the pleural layers describes pleural effusion.
Correct. The book describes fibrotic tissue replacing normal lung, which lowers compliance, increases elastic recoil and raises the work of breathing.
questions.clue: Restrictive disease with scarred alveoli.
questions.priority: Link fibrosis pathophysiology to the client's dyspnea.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic finding is most consistent with pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Chest x-ray showing hyperinflation and a flat diaphragm
Lateral decubitus film with layering fluid
High-resolution CT showing honeycombing and scarring
Positive sputum acid-fast bacilli
rationales: Incorrect. Hyperinflation with a flat diaphragm describes emphysema.
Incorrect. Layering fluid describes pleural effusion.
Correct. The book states high-resolution CT detects honeycombing, scarring and distorted lung structures.
Incorrect. A positive AFB sputum describes active TB.
questions.clue: Honeycombing on HRCT.
questions.priority: Recognize the imaging pattern of fibrosis.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary fibrosis has hypoxia and a prescription for low-flow oxygen. The nurse finds the client on a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min that was started without a new order. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave the non-rebreather on, since more oxygen is always better
Remove all oxygen until the provider arrives
Raise the flow on the non-rebreather further
Change to the prescribed low-flow oxygen, within 2 to 4 L/min, and reassess the client
rationales: Incorrect. The device does not match the prescription or the book's low-flow approach.
Incorrect. Removing oxygen from a hypoxic client is unsafe.
Incorrect. This moves further from the prescribed therapy.
Correct. The book lists low-flow oxygen at 2 to 4 L/min for hypoxia in fibrosis; the nurse corrects the setup to match the order and checks the client's response.
questions.clue: Oxygen device does not match the low-flow prescription.
questions.priority: Give oxygen safely, as prescribed.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with pulmonary fibrosis how to avoid worsening of the disease. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Get the flu and pneumococcal vaccines
Use as much oxygen as you can tolerate
Avoid smoke and air pollutants
Keep working with silica dust if you wear a cloth mask
Avoid people who have infections
rationales: Correct. The book says to encourage flu and pneumococcal vaccines.
Incorrect. The book calls for low-flow oxygen if needed.
Correct. The book says to avoid exposure to smoke and pollutants.
Incorrect. Silica is a listed occupational cause; ongoing exposure is harmful.
Correct. The book says to avoid exposure to infections.
questions.clue: Avoid smoke, pollutants and infections; get vaccinated.
questions.priority: Prevent further lung injury and infection.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary fibrosis is starting nintedanib. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?
options: "This medicine will cure my lung disease."
"This medicine removes the extra fluid from my legs."
"This medicine stops wheezing within minutes."
"This medicine slows the cells that cause scarring in my lungs."
rationales: Incorrect. The book states there is no cure except lung transplant.
Incorrect. Diuretics treat fluid from cor pulmonale.
Incorrect. Quick relief of wheezing describes a bronchodilator.
Correct. The book states nintedanib slows fibroblast activity.
questions.clue: Nintedanib is an antifibrotic.
questions.priority: Evaluate understanding of antifibrotic therapy and its limits.

questions.stem: The nurse takes a history from a client newly diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis. Which conditions does the book list as causes of pulmonary fibrosis? Select all that apply.
options: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Myasthenia gravis
Scoliosis
Well-controlled hypertension
Ankylosing spondylitis
rationales: Correct. Neuromuscular diseases including ALS are listed.
Incorrect. Seasonal allergies are not listed.
Correct. Myasthenia gravis is a listed neuromuscular cause.
Correct. Scoliosis is a listed spinal deformity.
Incorrect. Hypertension is not listed as a cause.
Correct. Ankylosing spondylitis is a listed spinal deformity.
questions.clue: Neuromuscular diseases and spinal deformities.
questions.priority: Recognize less obvious causes of pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary fibrosis has several medications. For each drug, indicate its purpose according to the book.
rationales: Nintedanib is an antifibrotic that slows fibroblast activity.
Pirfenidone is an antifibrotic that reduces scarring and inflammation.
The book lists diuretics to manage cor pulmonale.
The book lists digitalis to manage cor pulmonale.
Bronchodilators are listed to improve airflow.
questions.clue: Collaborative care drug list.
questions.priority: Match each drug to its role in fibrosis care.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with pulmonary fibrosis. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with new jugular vein distention, leg edema and worsening hypoxia
A client with long-standing finger clubbing and a stable SpO2
A client with a dry cough that is unchanged since admission
A client who wants to learn energy conservation techniques
rationales: Correct. JVD, edema and worsening hypoxia are new signs of cor pulmonale and respiratory decline, which need prompt assessment.
Incorrect. Clubbing is a chronic finding, and the client is stable.
Incorrect. An unchanged dry cough is expected.
Incorrect. Teaching is important but can follow assessment of the unstable client.
questions.clue: New cor pulmonale signs with worsening hypoxia.
questions.priority: Prioritize new, worsening findings over chronic stable ones.

questions.stem: A client admitted after a rib fracture suddenly develops distended neck veins, hypotension, tachycardia and a trachea shifted away from the injured side. What should the nurse do first?
options: Document the findings and recheck vital signs in 1 hour
Give a PRN pain medication and reassess in 30 minutes
Call for emergency help and notify the provider immediately while staying with the client
Place the client flat and leave to get the chest tube supplies
rationales: Incorrect. Waiting an hour delays treatment of a life-threatening problem.
Incorrect. Pain medication does not treat trapped air pressing on chest structures.
Correct. These are signs of tension pneumothorax, which the book calls a medical emergency; the nurse summons help at once and stays with the client.
Incorrect. Lying flat does not help, and leaving the client alone is unsafe.
questions.clue: Tension pneumothorax signs after chest trauma.
questions.priority: Escalate a tension pneumothorax immediately.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the chest tube system of a client with a pneumothorax. Which finding needs to be corrected?
options: The drainage collection chamber is below the level of the chest
The tube is not clamped
The tubing hangs in a dependent loop below the bed
There is no bubbling in the water seal chamber
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to keep the collection chamber lower than the chest.
Incorrect. The book says to clamp only when changing the system, with a physician order.
Correct. The book states the tubing should have no dependent loops.
Incorrect. The book states bubbling in the water seal is not normal and signals an air leak.
questions.clue: Chest tube tubing setup.
questions.priority: Keep the chest drainage system working safely.

questions.stem: A client has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax estimated at 30%. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
options: Needle aspiration alone
Observation without oxygen
Thrombolytic therapy
Aspiration with a pigtail catheter plus low suction or water seal
rationales: Incorrect. Needle aspiration is listed for a pneumothorax under 20% with symptoms.
Incorrect. A pneumothorax over 20% needs evacuation; oxygen is part of care.
Incorrect. Thrombolytics treat clots, not pneumothorax.
Correct. The book lists aspiration with a pigtail catheter and low suction or water seal for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax greater than 20%.
questions.clue: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax larger than 20%.
questions.priority: Anticipate treatment based on pneumothorax size.

questions.stem: For each description, indicate which of the three primary forms of pneumothorax it describes.
rows: Rupture of air sacs without injury
Trapped air applying potentially lethal pressure to chest structures
rationales: Spontaneous pneumothorax is non-traumatic, often from ruptured air sacs.
A rib fracture is a listed example of traumatic pneumothorax.
A stab injury is a listed example of traumatic pneumothorax.
Tension pneumothorax is the emergency in which trapped air puts lethal pressure on thoracic structures.
questions.clue: Three primary forms of pneumothorax.
questions.priority: Classify the pneumothorax to anticipate urgency and treatment.

questions.stem: A client with a pneumothorax larger than 20% has a chest tube placed. Which finding best shows that the treatment is working?
options: Breath sounds return on the affected side as the lung re-expands
The trachea newly shifts away from the affected side
Dyspnea increases over the next hour
Continuous bubbling appears in the water seal chamber
rationales: Correct. The book states the chest tube re-establishes negative pleural pressure and the nurse monitors for lung re-expansion.
Incorrect. Tracheal deviation away from the affected side signals tension pneumothorax.
Incorrect. Worsening dyspnea shows the problem is not resolving.
Incorrect. The book states bubbling in the water seal signals an air leak.
questions.clue: Chest tube to re-establish negative pleural pressure.
questions.priority: Evaluate re-expansion after chest tube placement.

questions.stem: A client with a chest tube for a large pneumothorax is taking shallow breaths and splinting the chest because of pain. What should the nurse do?
options: Clamp the chest tube to reduce pain
Give the prescribed PRN pain medication and reassess breathing
Remove the supplemental oxygen to make the client more comfortable
Encourage the client to avoid deep breaths until the tube is removed
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to clamp only when changing the system, with a physician order.
Correct. The book lists treating pain PRN in clients with a pneumothorax greater than 20%; pain control lets the client breathe more deeply.
Incorrect. Supplemental oxygen is part of the book's treatment.
Incorrect. Shallow breathing is the problem; pain control supports better breathing.
questions.clue: Pain limiting breathing with a chest tube.
questions.priority: Treat pain so the client can breathe effectively.

questions.stem: A client with active TB must go to radiology for a test. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Have the client wear a mask during transport
Remove all precautions once the client leaves the room
Give the client tissues instead of a mask
Send the client with family members instead of staff
rationales: Correct. The book's infection prevention measures for TB include masks, cough etiquette and hand hygiene.
Incorrect. TB spreads by airborne droplets; precautions continue outside the room.
Incorrect. The book lists masks; tissues alone are not enough.
Incorrect. This does not prevent spread and leaves the client without staff support.
questions.clue: Active TB leaving the isolation room.
questions.priority: Prevent airborne spread during transport.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with active pulmonary TB. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Weight gain
Night sweats
Hemoptysis
Improved appetite
Lymphadenopathy
Fatigue and activity intolerance
rationales: Incorrect. The book lists weight loss, not gain.
Correct. Night sweats are a listed symptom.
Correct. Hemoptysis is a listed finding.
Incorrect. The book lists anorexia and altered taste.
Correct. Lymphadenopathy is a listed finding.
Correct. Fatigue, weakness and activity intolerance are listed.
questions.clue: TB assessment infographic.
questions.priority: Recognize the systemic and respiratory signs of TB.

questions.stem: A client is being evaluated for TB. For each test, indicate how the book describes its purpose.
rationales: The Mantoux test screens for TB exposure.
The HIV test screens for immunosuppression risk.
Sputum AFB is positive in active TB; three samples are typically collected.
Blood and urine cultures detect systemic or extrapulmonary TB.
Biopsy identifies granulomas or bacilli.
questions.clue: Screening tests versus tests that find the disease.
questions.priority: Know what each TB test can and cannot tell you.

questions.stem: A client with drug-resistant TB asks how long the treatment will last. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Treatment lasts 2 weeks, until your cough stops."
"Treatment for drug-resistant TB can last up to 24 months."
"Treatment is the same 6 weeks as for any TB."
"You can stop as soon as one sputum test is negative."
rationales: Incorrect. TB treatment lasts months, not weeks.
Correct. The book states standard therapy is 6 to 9 months and up to 24 months for drug-resistant TB.
Incorrect. Even standard therapy is 6 to 9 months, and resistant TB is longer.
Incorrect. Medication adherence through the full course is essential.
questions.clue: Drug-resistant TB.
questions.priority: Prepare the client for a long course to support adherence.

questions.stem: A client with active TB says, "I don't know how I'll remember all these pills every day for months." The client lives with a spouse. Which nursing action best supports the client?
options: Tell the client it is fine to stop once the cough is gone
Teach the client and spouse together about the treatment, its complications, and why adherence matters
Suggest taking the pills only on days the client feels sick
Keep the spouse out of teaching to protect the client's privacy
rationales: Incorrect. Stopping early contradicts the book's emphasis on adherence.
Correct. The book calls for educating the client and family about treatment, complications and adherence; involving the spouse gives the client support.
Incorrect. Skipping doses undermines treatment.
Incorrect. The book directs teaching to the patient and family.
questions.clue: The client is worried about a long treatment and has family at home.
questions.priority: Use family support to promote adherence and coping.

questions.stem: A client hospitalized with TB has anorexia, weight loss and altered taste. Which intervention addresses these findings?
options: Restrict fluids to reduce secretions
Provide nutritional support
Keep the client NPO to rest the gut
Increase activity to stimulate the appetite
rationales: Incorrect. Fluid restriction does not address poor nutrition; the book lists IV fluids as supportive care.
Correct. The book lists nutritional support as supportive care and nutrition under support for recovery.
Incorrect. Withholding food worsens weight loss.
Incorrect. The book promotes rest and assistance with self-care during recovery.
questions.clue: Anorexia and weight loss in TB.
questions.priority: Support recovery with adequate nutrition.

questions.stem: The family of a client with active TB asks how TB spreads. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: "It spreads mainly by touching the client's skin."
"It spreads when people breathe in droplets from the air."
"It usually takes sustained, close contact to catch it."
"It spreads only through contact with blood."
"The bacteria tend to settle in well-ventilated areas of the lungs."
rationales: Incorrect. TB is spread through the air, not by skin contact.
Correct. The book describes airborne transmission by inhaling M. tuberculosis droplets.
Correct. The book states transmission usually requires sustained contact.
Incorrect. TB is airborne, not bloodborne.
Correct. The book notes bacilli implant in well-ventilated (high-oxygen) areas of the lungs.
questions.clue: Airborne droplets and prolonged exposure.
questions.priority: Teach accurate transmission facts to protect the family.

questions.stem: Four clients arrive at a walk-in clinic. Which client should the nurse place in an airborne isolation room first?
options: A client with asthma who is wheezing after exercise
A healthcare worker with no symptoms who is here for annual TB screening
A client recently released from prison who has a productive cough, hemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss
A client with a sore throat and runny nose for two days
rationales: Incorrect. Exercise-induced wheezing points to asthma.
Incorrect. A screening visit without symptoms does not need isolation first.
Correct. Incarceration is a listed TB risk, and cough, hemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss are listed TB findings.
Incorrect. These symptoms do not suggest active TB.
questions.clue: Risk history plus classic TB symptoms.
questions.priority: Isolate the client most likely to have active TB first.

questions.stem: A client's nasal cannula is set at 8 L/min. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave it, since higher flow gives more oxygen safely through any device
Increase it to 10 L/min to reach 60% oxygen
Switch the client to room air until the provider calls back
Recognize that this is above the nasal cannula range and contact the provider about a different device
rationales: Incorrect. The nasal cannula is used at 1 to 6 L/min.
Incorrect. Going higher moves further outside the cannula range.
Incorrect. Removing oxygen from a client who needs it is unsafe.
Correct. The book lists the nasal cannula range as 1 to 6 L/min; higher needs call for a different device.
questions.clue: Nasal cannula flow above 6 L/min.
questions.priority: Use oxygen devices within their correct flow range.

questions.stem: For each set of ABG results, indicate the interpretation.
rows: pH 7.49, PaCO2 41 mm Hg, HCO3 31 mEq/L
pH 7.40, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L
pH 7.30, PaCO2 39 mm Hg, HCO3 17 mEq/L
pH 7.52, PaCO2 44 mm Hg, HCO3 34 mEq/L
rationales: High pH with a high HCO3 and normal PaCO2 is metabolic alkalosis.
pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 are all within the book's normal ranges.
Low pH with a low HCO3 and normal PaCO2 is metabolic acidosis.
High pH with a high HCO3 and normal PaCO2 is metabolic alkalosis.
questions.clue: HCO3 (22-26 mEq/L) reflects the metabolic component.
questions.priority: Interpret ABGs step by step: pH, PaCO2, then HCO3.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews respiratory rates for several clients. Which clients need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: An adult breathing 16/min
A school-age child breathing 36/min
An infant breathing 40/min
An adult breathing 24/min
An infant breathing 68/min
A child breathing 26/min
rationales: Incorrect. 16/min is within the adult range of 12 to 20.
Correct. 36/min is above the child range of 20 to 30.
Incorrect. 40/min is within the infant range of 30 to 60.
Correct. 24/min is above the adult range of 12 to 20.
Correct. 68/min is above the infant range of 30 to 60.
Incorrect. 26/min is within the child range of 20 to 30.
questions.clue: Normal respiratory rate ranges by age.
questions.priority: Compare each rate with the normal range for age.

questions.stem: A client who is short of breath has slid down and is slumped low in the bed. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Lower the bed flat
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Turn the client prone
Elevate the head of the bed
rationales: Incorrect. Lying flat makes breathing harder.
Incorrect. A head-down position works against breathing.
Incorrect. Prone positioning is not the book's general measure to ease breathing.
Correct. The book lists elevating the head of the bed to ease breathing as a respiratory nursing priority.
questions.clue: Slumped, dyspneic client.
questions.priority: Raise the head of the bed to ease breathing.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews ABG results for four clients. Which result needs follow-up first?
options: pH 7.38, PaCO2 42 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L, PaO2 62 mm Hg
pH 7.41, PaCO2 39 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L, PaO2 94 mm Hg
pH 7.36, PaCO2 44 mm Hg, HCO3 23 mEq/L, PaO2 88 mm Hg
pH 7.44, PaCO2 36 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L, PaO2 98 mm Hg
rationales: Correct. A PaO2 of 62 mm Hg is below the 80 to 100 mm Hg range and indicates hypoxemia.
Incorrect. All values are within the normal ranges.
Incorrect. All values are within the normal ranges.
Incorrect. All values are within the normal ranges.
questions.clue: PaO2 below 80 mm Hg.
questions.priority: Act on hypoxemia first (ABCs).

questions.stem: The nurse checks oxygen setups for several clients. For each setup, indicate whether it is correct or needs correction.
rows: Heated, humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 50 L/min for a client with severe hypoxemia
Nasal cannula at 4 L/min for a client with mild hypoxia who is eating
Bag-valve mask at 15 L/min for emergency manual ventilation
rationales: The book lists 6 to 15 L/min for a partial rebreather; 3 L/min is too low.
HFNC runs up to 60 L/min, heated and humidified, for severe cases.
The nasal cannula runs at 1 to 6 L/min for mild hypoxia and lets the client talk and eat.
The book lists the BVM at 15 L/min for emergency manual ventilation.
questions.clue: Oxygen device flow ranges.
questions.priority: Match each oxygen device to its correct flow and use.

concerns.issue: States patients 'tend to tolerate a pH <7.2' with rising PaCO2, which contradicts page 16 ('Permissive hypercapnia acceptable if pH > 7.2').
'PEEP usually 15 cm H2O or greater' is stated as a general rule for ARDS; this is an overgeneralization since PEEP is titrated (as page 16 itself says).
Typo 'surface tention'; also the PEEP rationale claims PEEP decreases surface tension, which is not its mechanism (surfactant affects surface tension; PEEP keeps alveoli open).

Physiology statement says the brainstem detects low PaO2 and peripheral regulation occurs in the aortic arch only; central chemoreceptors respond mainly to CO2/pH, and the carotid bodies (main peripheral oxygen sensors) are omitted.
'Low PaCO2 is the primary drive for breathing for these patients' is incorrect; it should be low PaO2 (hypoxic drive), and it contradicts page 15.
Typos: 'FEV,/FVC' should be FEV1/FVC; 'a-1 antitrypsindeficiency' missing space; 'Corticosteroids Antibiotics (if increased mucus production)' runs two items together.
Warfarin target INR listed as 2.5-3.5 for PE/VTE; the usual VTE target is 2.0-3.0.

Pneumonia definition: 'micromutant' appears to be a typo for microorganism; 'lung interstitial' should be interstitium; 'lobular pneumonia' for part of a lobe and 'lobar pneumonia' for an entire lung are mislabeled (lobar pneumonia involves a lobe).
Diagnosis table lists 'Egophony or fluid collection' as the abnormal thoracentesis fluid result; egophony is an auscultation finding, not a fluid result. Also 'Bloud Gases' typo.
Pulmonary embolism section has no 'A2. Pulmonary embolism' heading; the section starts directly with Table 2.
Section numbering is inconsistent: Asthma (p27), Emphysema (p32) and Pulmonary Fibrosis (p34) lack A6/A8/A9 labels while other sections are numbered.

Asthma classification thresholds overlap or are inconsistent (mild intermittent '<2x/week' vs mild persistent '2x/week'); 'percusion' and 'suprac-clavicular' typos; vocal fremitus listed among asthma signs is questionable.
Status asthmaticus diagnostic table repeats the 'Fatigue/Lethargy/Confusion' row twice.

The Remember box in the pleural effusion section (avoid high O2 flow, monitor for respiratory acidosis, small high-calorie meals, vaccines) is identical to the emphysema box on page 34 and appears misplaced for pleural effusion.
'Four Types of Emphysema' lists bronchiectasis as an emphysema type; bronchiectasis is a separate airway disease, not a type of emphysema.
Pulmonary fibrosis PFTs listed as small airway obstruction and increased residual volume (air trapping), which contradicts the page 34 description of fibrosis as a restrictive disease.
Pneumothorax infographic is titled 'Two Types of Pneumothorax' while page 36 states there are three primary forms.
Venturi mask row places '24-60%' (an FiO2 value) in the Flow column instead of a flow rate.
Typos in cheat sheet: 'pneumoia' in auscultation sounds; 'confussion' on page 38 TB assessment.

'Avoid triggers (allergens, cold, exercise, NSAIDs)' tells clients with asthma to avoid exercise, which conflicts with the same page's use of albuterol before exercise; exercise is usually pre-treated rather than avoided.
Level-of-care thresholds 'PFR < 50% admit to ICU / PFR > 50 -70% admit to telemetry' use unclear notation and are not a widely standardized rule.
'Increase I/E 1:3-4' / 'Increase I/E ratio to prevent auto-PEEP' is ambiguous; the intent is to lengthen expiratory time (I:E 1:3 to 1:4). Not used as a keyed item.
Emphysema risk factor 'Substance use (e.g. cocaine, IV methadone(methylphenidate))' is garbled; IV methylphenidate use is the recognized association.
Independent nursing actions infographic repeats 'Educate on disease, lifestyle changes, and avoiding irritants' twice; 'occupational/role loss Suicide risk' runs two items together.

Drug mechanisms table describes ethambutol as 'inhibits bacterial metabolite production' and PZA as 'bacteriostatic/cidal; disrupts cell metabolism', which are vague or imprecise (ethambutol inhibits cell wall arabinogalactan synthesis). ETB and PZA mechanisms were not used in items.

ABG interpretation table shows compensatory arrows (e.g., HCO3 up in respiratory acidosis, PaCO2 down in metabolic acidosis) without labeling them as compensation, which can confuse students; items use uncompensated values.
ABG box lists 'PaO2 < 80 mm Hg, SaO2 < 95%' as ARDS diagnostic values; these are nonspecific, and ARDS hypoxemia is defined by the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (page 17).

blueprint: resp chapter has 8 psych (target 9) and 8 bcc (target 9) items; psychosocial and basic-care content in this chapter is limited, so rrp (13) and pa (14) are one over target. All within validator tolerance.

Chest tube box says any bubbling in the water seal chamber 'is not normal; it is a sign of an air leak.' Intermittent bubbling while a pneumothorax is still being evacuated can be expected; continuous bubbling is the air-leak sign. v3 items use only 'continuous bubbling' or 'no bubbling' and do not rely on the overgeneralization.

Pharmacology table says warfarin is 'started after heparin', while page 19 says to initiate Coumadin on the first treatment day if possible; the two statements read as inconsistent. No v3 item uses warfarin timing.
